etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from earlier あしこ (ashiko). The asoko form appears in the Utsubo Monogatari of the late 900s, during the Heian period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English yacht, from Dutch jacht.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Reduplication of 一人(ひとり) (hitori, “one person”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 値(ね) (ne, “price”) + 段(だん) (dan, “level”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle Chinese 分解

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Classical Japanese verb 加(くは)ふ (kufafu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with Japanese 進(すす)める (susumeru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 庖丁 (baew teng, “cook”).
包 is a daiyōji replacing 庖.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Chinese 同一 (duwng + ʔjit, literally “same + one”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Nominalization of the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 帰(かえ)る (kaeru, “to return”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/sakipapi/ → /sakiɸaɸi/ → /sakiwawi/ → /sakiwai/ → /saiwai/
Derived from sakiwai below.
Most often spelled as 幸い with the final い to indicate the reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/sakipapi/ → /sakiɸaɸi/ → /sakiwahi/ → /sakiwai/
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 幸う (sakiwau, “to meet with good fortune; to prosper”), itself a compound of 幸 (saki, “good fortune, happiness”) + 這う (hau, “to spread out widely”).
Most often spelled as 幸い with the final い to indicate the reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/sat͡ɕipapi/ → /sat͡ɕiɸaɸi/ → /sat͡ɕiwahi/ → /sat͡ɕiwai/
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 幸う (sachiwau, “to meet with good fortune; to prosper”), itself a compound of 幸 (sachi, “good fortune, happiness”) + 這う (hau, “to spread out widely”).
Most often spelled as 幸い with the final い to indicate the reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Calque of Dutch aantrekkingskracht (“attraction force”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 意 (MC 'iH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From the Classical Japanese verb せむ (semu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Cognate with 責(せ)める (semeru), 迫(せま)る (semaru), 狭(せば)める (sebameru), 狭(せば)まる (sebamaru), and 狭(せま)い (semai).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Reduplication of 方(かた) (kata, “person”). The kata changes to gata as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 書籍 (MC syo dzjek).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Kojiki of 712 and the Man'yōshū of 759. In turn, from Proto-Japonic *matu.
Various theories exist regarding its ultimate origin:
* Might be a shift from 保つ (tamotsu, “to hold”). However, the accent of 保つ (tamotsu) in the Heian period is HHL, while 松 (matsu) is LH. It can be better derived from 持つ (motsu, “to hold, to carry”), which has LF accent in the Heian period.
* Might be from 待つ (matsu, “to wait”), either from the way that a pine tree must wait for leaves to fall to grow new ones, or from the way that it lasts ten thousand years and preserves its color. The accent of 待つ (matsu) is LF.
* Possibly derived from 全く (mataku, “entirely”), from 全い (matai, “complete”), because it spends its time in the snow for winter. However, the classical term 全し (matasi) is HHF in the Heian period.
* From 睫毛 (matsuge, “eyelashes”), since their leaves represent such. However, it requires deletion of the -ge, and matsuge is certainly from 目 (ma-, “eye”).
* From 真常木 (matonoki, “true eternal tree”), as the pine tree is an evergreen tree.
* From a place name 松のむらたち (MATSU no muratachi), as opposed to muratatsu.
* From 芽厚 (meatsu, literally “buds (are) thick”).
* From 纏わる (matsuwaru, “get wrapped around”), as the leaves are around the trunk.
* From 真 (ma-, “true”) + つ (tsu, abbreviation of 約まる (tsuzumaru, “to shrink”)).
* From 間千 (machi, literally “space (of) thousands”).
* A shift from 股 (mata, “crouch”), as the pine tree leaves split into two.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 灰(はい) (hai, “ash”) + 色(いろ) (-iro, “color”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Sino-Japonic compound word from Middle Chinese 皮 (MC bje) and Middle Chinese 膚 (MC pju). First attested in 717. Compare Korean 피부 (pibu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kami₂⟩ → */kamɨ/ → /kami/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kamui.
Not related to 上 (kami₁ → kami, “top, upper”) or 髪 (kami, “hair”).
Often appears in compounds as kamu- or kan-, indicating that kami is an unbound form deriving from */kamui/. Such apophony has occurred in other Japanese terms, such as 目 (me, ma-, “eye”) or 酒 (sake, saka-, “sake, liquor”). See also WT:AJPX#Standalone forms and combining forms.
Compare Korean 검 (geom, “god, spirit”) and Ainu カムイ (kamuy, “god”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 神 (MC zyin). Compare modern Mandarin 神 (shén).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 神 (MC zyin).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨mi₁⟩ → */mʲi/ → /mi/
From Old Japanese.
Cognate with 御 (mi-), an honorific prefix originally used to refer to gods and other high-status objects.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shortened from 禅那 (zenna, “Zen meditation practice”), from Middle Chinese 禪那 (MC dzyen na), a transliteration of Sanskrit ध्यान (dhyāna, “profound meditation”). Compare Pali jhāna.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 福 (MC pjuwk).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Coined by Japanese philosopher Inoue Tetsujirō in 1881 in his work 哲学字彙 (Tetsugaku Jii, “Dictionary of Philosophy”) as a calque of English absolute, based on the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra (《法華玄義》), changing the spelling from 絶待 to 絶対.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tuna.
First attested in the Harima Fudoki of 715 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 綱 (MC kang). Compare Korean 강 (gang).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears in the Wamyō Ruijushō of 938 CE.
Compound of 羽(は) (ha, “feather”, see below) + 根(ね) (ne, “root”), originally referring specifically to where the quill of a feather attaches to the skin. Over time, the meaning broadened to refer to a feather, and from there, to refer to a wing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
May be cognate with 葉(は) (ha, “leaf”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 羽 (MC hjuX|hjuH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 落(お)とす (otosu) + 物(もの) (-mono)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alteration of shunyū below, using the kan'yōon of yu for the 輸 character.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ɕunipu/ → /ɕuniɸu/ → /ɕuniwu/ → /ɕuniu/ → /ɕunjuː/
From Middle Chinese compound 輸入 /输入 (syu nyip, literally “to convey + to enter, to go in”).
This reading has been replaced by the yunyū reading above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 送(そう) (sō) + 料(りょう) (-ryō)
